title: Looking at the Cat's Eye Nebula with Hubble
caption: The Cat's Eye Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6543, Cat's Eye Nebula · constellation Draco · about 4400 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Month (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Rings within rings, fine jets and bright knots fill the core of the Cat's Eye Nebula, one of the most intricate planetary nebulae known. This view comes from the High Resolution Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and ESA/Hubble calls it the sharpest image yet of the nebula.

A planetary nebula is the gas a dying star sheds as it nears the end of its life. The Cat's Eye has a special place in that story: in 1864, its light, split into a spectrum, helped show astronomers that these objects are clouds of expanding gas rather than distant stars.

The concentric shells may be a record of the central star losing mass in episodes rather than all at once, while the jets and the knots shaped by shock waves trace faster, more violent outflows. The image combines archival Hubble data that had never been used with new processing.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys (High Resolution Channel) observed the nebula through narrowband filters for nitrogen, oxygen and ionized nitrogen. ESA/Hubble has not published which color each filter was given.
understand.eye: Narrowband filters isolate the glow of single elements, so the colors are a map of chemistry rather than what an eye would see.

explore: Its distance of about 4,400 light-years comes from ESA's Gaia mission. Hubble's first images of the nebula, in 1995, were the ones that revealed its complex structure; this release revisits it with data that had gone unused until now.
sources: NASA: Two Observatories, One Cosmic Eye
alt: The layered core of the Cat's Eye Nebula, with concentric shells, jets and bright knots of gas.
